title: Why multilinear maps
promptMarkdown: In under 200 words, and without the notes open, explain why this course defines tensors as multilinear maps on vectors and one-forms rather than as 'arrays of numbers with indices'. Say what frame independence buys for physics, using the number-flux 4-vector and its conservation law $\partial_\mu N^\mu = 0$ as the example, and state one thing that the component definition gets right that beginners often miss.
hintLadder: If a law is written as an equation between tensors and holds in one inertial frame, what can you conclude about other frames?
What does $N^\mu$ mean geometrically, and what do its components mean to a particular observer?

criteria.criterion: Explains that a tensor is a single geometric object whose components are its values on basis vectors/one-forms, so a tensor equation true in one frame is true in all (frame independence of physical laws).
N^μ = n u^μ: n and u^μ are geometric; N⁰ and N^i are what an observer calls density and flux; ∂_μ N^μ = 0 is one scalar equation that every observer reads as a continuity equation.
Names a correct insight of the component definition: the transformation law is the content (four numbers do not make a vector), or index placement encodes which argument slot is meant.
